senses.text: alphabetical letter The first letter of the alphabet [according to the order in which the letters are now commonly disposed; and also according to the original order, which see in art. Abjd ]: called A^alifN . [This name, like most of the other names of Arabic letters, is traceable to the Phœnician language, in which it signifies “an ox;” the ancient Phœnician form of the letter thus called being a rude representation of an ox's head.] It is, of all the letters, that which is most frequent in speech: and some say that, in A=l=m= , in the Kur [ch. ii. &c.], it is a name of God. (TA.) Its name is properly fem., as is also that of every other letter; [and hence its pl. is A^alifaAtN ;] but it may be made masc.: so says Ks: Sb says that all the letters of the alphabet are masc. and fem., like

15 and 18]: in the other case as in DarabotuhaA and mararotu bihaA . (T.) The difference between it and A^alifu AlwaSoli is, that the latter is in the beginnings of nouns and verbs, and the former is in the endings of nouns [and verbs]. (T, K.) It is also called A^alifu AlA_iTolaAqi [ The alif of unbinding, because the vowel ending a rhyme prevents its being muqay~d , i. e. “bound” by the preceding consonant]: (Mughnee;) and A^alifu AlfaASilapi [ the alif of the final word of a verse of poetry or of a verse of the Kur-án or of a clause of rhyming prose ]. senses.text: The first of a series of eight words comprising the letters of the Arabic alphabet [ in the order in which they were originally disposed, agreeing with that of the Hebrew and Aramaic, but with six additional letters: they are variously written and pronounced; generally as follows: A^abojada haw~azo HuT~iY kalamano saEofaSo qara$ato vaxa*o DaZago : but the Arabs of Western Africa write the latter four thus: SEfD qrst vx* Zg$ ]: (K and TA in art. bjd : [in both of which are related several fables concerning the origin of these words:]) accord. to the general opinion, the word Abjd is of foreign origin, [like each of the words following it,] and therefore its first letter [as well as each of the others] is a radical. (TA.) [

Hence, AlA^abojadu signifies The alphabet. You say Huruwfu AlA^abojadi The letters of the alphabet. ― -b2- It is probable (as De Sacy has observed in his Ar. Gram., 2nd ed., i. 8,) that the Arabic alphabet originally consisted of only twenty-two letters: for some of the ancient Arabs called Saturday Abjd , Sunday hwz~ , and so on to qr$t inclusive; calling Friday Earuwbapu . ― -b3- In the lexicon entitled “El-'Eyn,” the letters of the alphabet are arranged nearly according to their places of utterance; as follows: E , H , h , x , g , q , k , j , $ , D , S , s , z , T , d , t , Z , * , v , r , l , n , f , b , m , w , A , Y : and this order has been followed in the Tahdheeb and Mohkam and some other lexicons.]

; (M, K;) by reason of pain: (S, TA:) he complained by reason of disease or pain: (TA:) he uttered a cry or cries: (Msb:) said of a man. (S, Msb.) ― -b2- A^an~iti Alqawosu , aor. tay^in~u , inf. n. A^aniynN , The bow made a gentle and prolonged sound. (AHn, M.) -A2- laA A^afoEaluhu maA A^an~a fiY Als~amaA='i najomN means I will not do it as long as there is a star in the heaven: (S, M, K:) A^an~a being here a dial. var. of Ean~a . (S.) You say also, maA A^an~a fiy AlfuraAti qaTorapN As long as there is a drop in the Euphrates. (T, S.) And laA A^afoEaluhu maA A^an~a fiY Als~amaA='N [ I will not do it as long as there is rain in the heaven ]. (S.) [It is said in the M that Lh mentions the last two sayings; but it is there indicated that he read qaTorapF and samaA='F : and] ISk mentions the s

is a pronoun, denoting the speaker, [ I, masc. and fem.,] in the language of some of the Arabs: they say, A^ano faEalotu [ I did ], with the n quiescent: but most of them pronounce it [↓ ] with fet-h when conjoined with a following word; (Mughnee, K;) saying, A^ana faEalotu : (TA:) and [↓ ] with A in a case of pause: (Mughnee, K:) and some pronounce it with A also when it is conjoined with a following word; saying, A^anaA faEalotu ; [as we generally find it written in books;] but this is of a bad dialect: (TA:) [this last assertion, however, requires consideration; for the dial. here said to be bad is that of Temeem, accord. to what here follows:] the Basrees hold that the pronoun consists of the ' and the n , and that the [final] A is redundant, because it is suppressed in a case of conju

; or it may be added to show what is the vowel, like the h , and be like the h in kitaAbiyaho and HisaAbiyahN . (M.) For the dual, as well as the pl., only naHonu is used. (Az, TA.) ― -b2- It is also a pronoun denoting the person addressed, or spoken to, by assuming the form ↓ [ Thou, masc.]; t being added to it as the sign of the person addressed, (S, M, Mughnee, K,) and A^ano being the pronoun, (M, Mughnee, K,) accord. to the general opinion; (Mughnee, K;) the two becoming as one; not that one is prefixed to the other as governing it in the gen. case: (S:) and so ↓ , (S, M, Mughnee, K,) addressed to the female: (S, M:) and ↓ , (M, Mughnee, K,) addressed to two; not a regular dual, for were it so it would be A^anotaAn ; but like kumaA in DarabotukumaA : (M:) and ↓ and ↓ , (S, Mughnee, K,)

]: (Mughnee, K: *) and in the phrase, balaganiY A^ano qado kaAna ka*aA wka*aA [ It has come to my knowledge, or been related to me, or been told to me, or it came to my knowledge, &c., that ( the case is this:) such and such things have been ]; a phrase of this kind, in which A^ano occurs with a verb, not being approved without qado , unless you say, balaganiY A^an~ahu kaAna ka*aA waka*aA : (Lth, T:) [for] when the contracted A^ano has for its predicate a verbal proposition, of which the verb is neither imperfectly inflected, like layosa and EasaY , nor expressive of a prayer or an imprecation, it is separated from the verb, according to the more approved usage, by qado , or the prefix sa , or sawofa , or a negative, as laA &c., or lawo : (I 'Ak pp.

100 and 101:) but when its predicate is a nominal proposition, it requires not a separation; so that you say, Ealimotu A^ano ziayodN qaAy^imN [ I knew that ( the case was this: ) Zeyd was standing ]; (I 'Ak p. 100;) and balaganiY A^ano zaydN xaArijN [ It has come to my knowledge, or been related to me, or been told to me, &c., that ( the case is this:) Zeyd is going, or coming, out, or forth ]; (TA;) except in the case of a negation, as in the saying in the Kur [xi. 17], wA^ano laA A_ilha A_il~aA huwa [ And that ( the case is this:) there is no deity but He ]. (I 'Ak p.

100.) Thus used, it is originally triliteral, and is also what is termed maSodariy~ap ; [ Ealima A^ano , in the first of the exs. above, for instance, meaning Ealima A^an~ahu , i. e. Ealima A^an~a Al$~aA^ona , which is equivalent to Ealima kawona Al$~aA^oni ;] and governs the subject in the accus. case, and the predicate in the nom. case: and its subject must be a pronoun, suppressed, [as in the exs. given above, where it means Al$~aA^oni , and in a verse cited before, commencing A^ano taqoraA=ni , accord. to A'boo-'Alee,] or expressed; the latter, accord. to the more correct opinion, being allowable only by poetic license: and its predicate must be a proposition, unless the subject is expressed, in which case it may be either a single word or a proposition; both of which kinds occur in th

104 of the Ar. text; and both are given in the S;) kaA^ano here meaning kaA^an~ahu ; and] Fr says, We have not heard the Arabs use the contracted form and make it to govern except with a pronoun, in which case the desinential syntax is not apparent. (T.) The author of the K says in the B that you say, Ealimotu A^ano zyodFA lamunoTaliqN [ I knew that Zeyd was indeed going away ], with l when it is made to govern; and Ealimotu A^ano zayodN munoTaliqN [ I knew that ( the case was this:) Zeyd was going away ], without l when it is made to have no government. (TA. [But in the latter ex. it governs the subject, which is understood, as in other exs. before given.]) [See an ex. in a verse ending with the phrase wakaA^ano qadi cited voce qad , where kaA^ano is for kaA^an~ahu , meaning kaA^an~a Al$~
; or yaquwlu , or yaquwluwna

; or some other form of the verb qaAla ; i. e. Saying ; &c.;] as in the saying [in the Kur xxiii. 27], faA^awoHayonaA A_ilayohi A^ani ASonaEi Aloquloka [ And we revealed, or spake by revelation, unto him, saying, Make thou the ark ]; (Mughnee, K) and [in the Kur vii. 41,] wanuwduwA A^ano tilokumu Alojan~apu [ And it shall be proclaimed to them, being said, That is Paradise ]

; or in these two instances it may be regarded as what is termed maSodariy~ap , by supposing the preposition [ bi ] understood before it, so that in the former instance it is the biliteral, because it is put before the imperative, and in the second it is the contraction of A^an~a because it is put before a nominal proposition; (Mughnee;) and [in the Kur xxxviii. 5,] waAnoTalaqa AlomalaA^u minohumo A^ani Amo$uwA (S, M, Mughnee) i. e. [ And the chief persons of them ] broke forth, or launched forth, with their tongues, or in speech, [saying,] Go ye on, or continue ye, in your course of action &c. (Mughnee.) For this usage of A^ano certain conditions are requisite : first, that it be preceded by a proposition : secondly, that it be followed by a proposition; so that you may not say, *akarotu

; or, if there be in it those letters, that the word which they compose shall be interpreted by another word; as in the saying, in the Kur [v, 117], maA qulotu lahumo A_il~aA maA A^amarotaniY bihi A^ani AEobuduwA All~`ha which may mean, as Z says, I have not commanded them [aught save that which Thou commandedst me, saying, Worship ye God ]; (Mughnee;) in which instance Fr says that it is an explicative : (T :) fifthly, that there be not a preposition immediately before it; for if you say, katabotu A_ilayohi biA^ani AfoEalo ka*aA , it is what is termed maSodariy~ap [as we have before shown]. (Mughnee.) When it may be regarded as an explicative and is followed by an aor. with lA as in A^a$arotu A_ilayohi A^ano laA tafoEal ka*aA , it may be marfooa, [namely, the aor.,] on the supposition tha

; or mejzoom, on the supposition that it is a prohibitive; and in both cases An is an explicative ; [so that the meaning is, I made a sign to him, as though saying, Thou wilt not do such a thing, in the former case

; or, in the latter, Do not thou such a thing ; ] or mansoob, on the supposition that lA is a negative and that An is what is termed maSodariy~ap : but if lA is wanting, it may not be mejzoom, but may be marfooa [if we use An as an explicative] or mansoob [if An be what is termed maSodariy~ap ]. (Mughnee.)― -b3- Fourthly, it is redundant, as a corroborative, (Mughnee, K,) like whatever else is redundant : and thus it is in four cases : one of these, which is the most common, being when it occurs after lam~aA denoting time; [and this is mentioned in the M ; ] as in the saying [in the Kur xxix. 32], walm~aA A^ano jaA='a to rusulunaA luwTFA [ And when our apostles came to Lot ]: (Mughnee:) [or,] accord. to J, (TA,) it is sometimes a connective to lam~aA ; as in the saying in the Kur [xii. 96]

is used in various ways: first, as a conditional particle, (S, M, Msb, Mughnee, K,) denoting the happening of the second of two events in consequence of the happening of the first, (S, Msb, *) whether the second be immediate or deferred, and whether the condition be affirmative or negative; (Msb;) [and as such it is followed by a mejzoom aor., or by a pret. having the signification of an aor.;] as in the saying, [ A_ino tafoEalN A^foEalN If thou do such a thing, I will do it; and] A_ino taA^otiniY A=tika [ If thou come to me, I will come to thee ]; and A_inN jiy^otaniY A^akoramotuka [ If thou come to me, I will treat thee with honour ]; (S;) and A_ino faEalota faEalotu [ If thou do, I will do ] for which the tribe of Teiyi say, as IJ relates on the authority of Ktr, hino faEalota faEalotu

19 of the same ch.,] waA_ino taEuwduwA naEudo [ But if ye return to attacking the Apostle, we will return to assisting him]. (Mughnee, K.) [On the difference between it and A_i*A , see the latter.] When either it or A_i*aA is immediately followed by a noun in the nom. case, the said noun is governed in that case by a verb necessarily suppressed, of which it is the agent; as in the saying, in the Kur [ix. 6], waA_ino A^aHadN mina A@lomu$orikiyna A@stajaAraka ; the complete phrase being waA_ini AsotajaAraka A^aHadN mina A@lomu$orikiyna A@sotajaAraka [ And if any one of the believers in a plurality of gods demand protection of thee, (if) he demand protection of thee ]: so accord. to the generality of the grammarians. (I 'Ak p.

123.) Sometimes it is conjoined with the negative laA , and the ignorant may imagine it to be the exceptive A_il~aA ; as in [the saying in the Kur ix. 40,] A_il~aA tanoSuruwhu faqad naSarahu A@ll~`hu [ If ye will not aid him, certainly God did aid him ]; and [in the next preceding verse,] A_il~aA tanofiruwA yuEa*~ibokumo [ If ye will not go forth to war, He will punish you ]. (Mughnee, K. *) It is sometimes used to denote one's feigning himself ignorant; as when you say to one who asks, “ Is thy child in the house? ” and thou hast knowledge thereof, A_ino kaAna fiY Ald~aAri A^aEolamotuka bihi [ If he be in the house, I will inform thee thereof ]. (Msb.) And to denote one's putting the knowing in the predicament of the ignorant, in order to incite to the doing or continuing an action; as wh

; or, whether he sit or not. (Msb.) [ A_im~aA as a compound of the conditional A_inN and the redundant maA , see in an art. of which AmA is the heading.] ― -b2- [Secondly,] it is a negative, (S, Mughnee, K,) syn. with maA ; (S;) and is put before a nominal proposition; (Mughnee, K;) as in the saying [in the Kur lxvii. 20], A_ini A@lokaAfiruwna A_il~aA fiY guruwrK [ The unbelievers are not in aught save in a deception ]; (S, Mughnee, K;) and before a verbal proposition; as in [the Kur ix. 108,] A_ino A^aradonaA A_il~aA A@loHusonaY [ We desired not, or meant not, aught save that which is best ]. (Mughnee, K.) The assertion of some, that the negative A_inN does not occur except where it is followed by A_il~aA , as in the instances cited above, or by lam~aA , with tesh-deed, which is syn. ther

69 and lxxii. 26], A_ino Eindakumo mino suloTaAnK bih`*aA [meaning, accord. to the Jel., Ye have no proof of this that ye say], and A_ino A^adoriyA^aqariybN maA tuwEaduwna [ I know not whether that with which ye are threatened be nigh ]. (Mughnee, K. *) The conditional and the negative both occur in the saying in the Kur [xxxv. 39], walay^ino zaAlataA A_ino A^amosakahumaA mino A^aHadK mino baEodihi [ And I swear that, if they should quit their place, not any one should withhold them after Him ]: the former is conditional; and the latter is negative, and is [part of] the complement of the oath which is denoted by the l prefixed to the former; the complement of the condition being necessarily suppressed. (Mughnee.) When it is put before a nominal proposition, it has no government, accord. to

34 accord. to one reading], waA_ino kul~u *`lika lamaA mataAEu A@loHayaApi A@ld~unoyaA [ And verily all that is the furniture of the present life ]; and, accord. to the reading of Hafs, [and of 'Ásim and Kh, in the Kur xx. 66, respecting which see A_in~a ,] A_ino h`*aAni lasaAHiraAni [ Verily these two are enchanters ]; &c. (Mughnee.) When it is put before a verbal proposition, it is necessarily made to have no government: (Mughnee, K:) and in most cases the verb is a preterite and of the kind called naAsix [which effects a change of the grammatical form or of the meaning in a nominal proposition before which it is placed]; as in the saying [in the Kur ii. 138], waA_ino kaAnatN lakabiyrapF [ And verily it was a great matter ]; and [in the Kur xvii. 75,] waA_ino kaAduwA layafotinuwnaka [ An

78 and 108: (T:) less frequently it is an aor. of a verb of this kind; as in the saying [in the Kur xxvi. 186], waA_ino naZun~uka lamina A@lokaA*ibyna [ And verily we think thee to be of the number of the liars ]: and both these kinds of expression may be taken as exs. to be imitated: less frequently than this it is a preterite of a verb not of the kind termed nasx ; as in the saying [of a poet], $al~atN yamiynuka A_inN qatalota lamusolimFA [ May thy right arm, or hand, dry up, or become unsound! verily thou hast slain a Muslim ]; but this may not be taken as an ex. to be imitated; contr. to the opinion of Akh; for he allows the phrase, A_ino qiAma laA^anaA [ Verily I stood ], and A_inN qaEada lA^anota [ Verily thou sattest ]: and less frequently than this it is an aor. of a verb not of th

99.) ― -b4- [Fourthly,] it is redundant, (S, Mughnee, K,) occurring with maA ; as in the saying, maA A_ino yaquwmu zayodN [ Zeyd does not stand ]; (S;) and in the saying [of a poet], kaA A_ino A^atayota bi$oY'K A^anota takorahuhu [ Thou didst not a thing which thou dislikest ]. (Mughnee, K: in the CK Aatotu .) It is mostly thus used after the negative mA , when put before a verbal proposition; as above

; or before a nominal proposition; as in the saying, manaAyaAnaA wadawolapu A=xariynaA wamaA A_ino Tib~unaA jbunN wl`kinN [ And our habit is not cowardice; but our destinies and the good fortune of others caused our being defeated]: and in this case it prevents the government of mA , as in this verse: but in the saying, baniY gudaAnapa maA A_ino A^anotumu *ahabFA walaA SariyfFA wal`kinN A^anotumu Alxazafu [ Sons of Ghudáneh, ye are not indeed gold, nor silver, or pure silver, but ye are pottery ], accord. to him who relates it thus, saying *hbFA and SryfFA , in the accus. case, it is explained as a negative, corroborative of mA : (Mughnee:) and accord. to J, (TA,) the negatives maA and A_inN are sometimes thus combined for corroboration; as in the saying of the rájiz, (El-Aghlab El-'Ijlee,

is one of the particles which annul the quality of the inchoative; and is originally A_in~a ; therefore Sb has not mentioned it among those particles [as distinct from A_in~a , from which, however, it is distinguished in meaning]: (I 'Ak p. 90:) it is a corroborative particle; (I 'Ak, Mughnee;) a particle governing the subject in the accus. case and the predicate in the nom. case, (S, I 'Ak, Mughnee, K,) combining with what follows it to form an equivalent to an inf. n., (S,) [for,] accord. to the most correct opinion, it is a conjunct particle, which, together with its two objects of government, is explained by means of an inf. n. (Mughnee.) If the predicate is derived, the inf. n. by means of which it is explained is of the same radical letters; so that the implied meaning of balaganiy A

91.) The former only may be used when the implied meaning is to be explained by an inf. n. (I 'Ak, K.) Such is the case when it occurs in the place of a noun governed by a verb in the nom. case; as in yuEojibuniY A^an~aka qaAy^imN [ It pleases me that thou art standing ], i. e. qiyaAmuka [ thy standing pleases me]: or in the place of a noun governed by a verb in the accus. case; as in Earafotu A^at~aka qaAy^imN [ I knew that thou wast standing ], i. e. qiyaAmaka [ thy standing ]: or in the place of a noun governed in the gen. case by a particle; as in Eajibotu mino A^an~aka qaAy^imN [ I wondered that thou wast standing ], i. e. mino qiyaAmka [ at, or by reason of, thy standing ]: (I 'Ak p. 91:) [and sometimes a preposition is understood; as in laA $ak~a A^an~ahu ka*aA , for laA $ak~a fiY A

305 and 306]. (K.) Sometimes its A^ is changed into E ; so that you say, Ealimotu Ean~aka munoTaliqN [meaning I knew that thou wast going away ]. (M.) ― -b2- With k prefixed to it, it is a particle of comparison, (S, * M, TA,) [still] governing the subject in the accus. case and the predicate in the nom. case: (TA:) you say, kaA^an~a zayodFA EamorNw [It is as though Zeyd were 'Amr ], meaning that Zeyd is like 'Amr; as though you said, A_in~a zayodFA kaAy^inN kaEamorKw [ verily, Zeyd is like 'Amr ]: [it is to be accounted for by an ellipsis: or] the k is taken away from the middle of this proposition, and put at its commencement, and then the kesreh of A_in~a necessarily becomes changed to a fet-hah, because A_in~a cannot be preceded by a preposition, for it never occurs but at the commence

; or the like: for] you say [also], kaA^an~iY bika meaning kaA^an~iY A^aboSuru bika [It is as though I saw thee ]; i. e. I know from what I witness of thy condition to-day how thy condition will be tomorrow; so that it is as though I saw thee in that condition: (Har p. 126: [see also bi ; near the end of the paragraph:]) [thus,] kaA^an~a also denotes knowing; and also thinking; [the former as in the saying immediately preceding, and] as when you say, kaA^an~a A@ll~`ha yafoEalu maA ya$aA='u [ I know, or rather it appears, as though seen, that God does what He wills ]; and [the latter as when you say,] kaA^an~aka xaArijN [ I think, or rather it seems, that Thou art going forth ]. (TA.) ― -b3- [When it has The affixed pronoun of the first person, sing. Or Pl., you say, A^an~iY and A^an~aniY ,
; or it is as thou sayest ]. (M, TA.) [See also A_in~a as exemplified by a verse commencing with wayaqulona and by a saying of Ibn-Ez-Zubeyr.]

is one of the particles which annul the quality of the inchoative, like A^an~a , of which it is the original: (I 'Ak p. 90:) it is a corroborative particle, (I 'Ak, Mughnee,) corroborating the predicate; (S, K;) governing the subject in the accus. case and the predicate in the nom. case; (S, I 'Ak, Mughnee, K;) [and may generally be rendered by Verily, or certainly, or the like; exactly agreeing with the Greek , as used in Luke vii.

16 and in many other passages in the New Testament; though it often seems to be nothing more than a sign of inception, which can hardly be rendered at all in English; unless in pronunciation, by laying a stress upon the predicate, or upon the copula;] as in the saying, A_in~a zayodFA qaAy^imN [ Verily, or certainly, Zeyd is standing
; or simply, Zeyd is standing, if we lay a stress upon standing, or upon is]. (I 'Ak p.

90.) But sometimes it governs both the subject and the predicate in the accus. case; as in the saying, A_i*aA A@$otad~a junoHu All~ayoli falotaA^oti walotakunN xuTaAka xifaAfFA A_in~a Hur~aAsanaA A^usodaA [ When the darkness of night becomes, or shall become, intense, then do thou come, and let thy steps be light: verily our guardians are lions ]; (Mughnee, K; [but in the latter, for A@$otad~a , we find A@sowad~a , so that the meaning is, when the first portion of the night becomes, or shall become, black, &c.;]) and as in a trad. in which it is said, An~a qaEora jahan~ama saboEiyna xariyfFA [ Verily the bottom of Hell is a distance of seventy years of journeying]: (Mughnee, K:) the verse, however, is explained by the supposition that it presents a denotative of state [in the last word, wh

The former must be used when it occurs inceptively, (Kh, T, I' Ak p. 92, Mughnee, K,) having nothing before it upon which it is syntactically dependent, (Kh, T,) with respect to the wording or the meaning; (K;) as in A_in~a zayodFA qaAy^imN [ Verily Zeyd is standing ]. (I' Ak, K.) It is used after A^alaA , (I' Ak, K,) the inceptive particle, (I' Ak,) or the particle which is employed to give notice [of something about to be said]; (K;) as in A^alaA A_in~a zayodFA qaAy^imN [ Now surely Zeyd is standing ]. (I' Ak K.) And when it occurs at the commencement of the complement of a conjunct noun; (I' Ak, K; *) as in jaA='a Al~a*iY A_in~ahu qaAy^imN [ He who is standing came ]; (I' Ak;) and in the Kur [xxviii. 76], waA=tayonaAhu mina A@lokunuwri maA A_in~a mafaAtiHahu latanuwo'u biA@loEuSoba

Also, when it occurs in a phrase denotative of state; (I' Ak;) [i. e.,] after the w denotative of state; (K;) as in zurotuhu waA_in~iY *uwA^amalK [ I visited him, I verily having hope, or expectation ]; (I' Ak;) and in jaA='a ziyodN wa A_in~a yadahu EalaY raA^osihi [ Zeyd came, he verily having his hand upon his head ]. (K.) And when it occurs in a phrase which is the predicate of a proper (as opposed to an ideal) substantive; (I' Ak, K; *) as in zayodN A_in~ahu qaAy^imN [ Zeyd, verily he is standing ], (I' Ak,) or *aAhibN [ going away ]; contr. to the assertion of Fr. (K.) And when it occurs before the l which suspends the grammatical government of a verb of the mind, preceding it, with respect to its objective complements; (I' Ak, K; *) as in Ealimotu A_in~a zayodFA laqaAy^imN [ I knew Z

Also, When it occurs after Hayovu ; as in Aijoliso Hayovu A_in~a zayodFA jaAlisN [ Sit thou where Zeyd is sitting ]. (I' Ak p. 92, and k) And after Hat~aY ; as in mariDa zayodN Hat~aY A_in~ahumo laA yarojuwnahu [ Zeyd has fallen sick, so that verily they have no hope for him : whereas after a particle governing the gen. case, [i. e. a preposition,] you say, ↓ . (IHsh in De Sacy's Anthol. Gr. Ar. P.

senses.text: 3 (S, Mgh, O, K) means The woman is on a par with the man to the third part of her bloodwit; (S, Mgh, O;) she receives like as the man receives [up to that point]: (Mgh:) i. e., [for instance,] his muwDiHap [or wound of the head for which the mulct is five camels] and her muwDiHap are equal; (K;) but when the portion reaches to the third of the bloodwit, her [portion of the] bloodwit is the half of that of the man: (S, O, K:) thus, for one of her fingers, ten camels are due to her, as in the case of the finger of the man; for two of her fingers, twenty camels; and for three of her fingers, thirty; but for four of her fingers, only twenty, because they exceed the third, therefore the portion is reduced to the half of what is due to the man: so accord. to Ibn-El-Museiyab: but Esh-Sháfi'ee an

; or by the abundance of the fruit of the trees, and the produce of the grains sown

; or by their being blessed with gardens of ripe fruits, so that they should gather them from the upper part of each tree, and pick up what should have fallen upon the ground. ; or does so in their absence: (TA:) and the action thus signified may be [ with words, or by making signs ] with the side of the mouth, and with the eye, and with the head. (TA in art. hmz .) 4 is from A^alaka signifying “he sent;” and is originally A^aA^olikoniY ; the [second] hemzeh being transposed and placed after the l , it becomes A^aloy^ikoniY ; then the hemzeh has its vowel transferred to the l and is thrown out; as is done in the case of malakN , which is originally maA^olakN , then maloA^akN , and then malakN : (IB in art. lwk :) it means Be thou my messenger; and bear thou my message; and is often used by the poets. (S in art. lwk .) Accord. to IAmb, one says, A^alikoniY A_ilaY fulaAnK , meaning send thou me to such a one: [but I do not know any instance in which this meaning is applicable:] and the original form is A^aloy^ikoniY

; or, if from AlA^aluwku , the original form is A^aA^olikoniY : and he also says that it means be thou my messenger to such a one. (TA.) One says also, A^alikoniY A_ilayohaA birisaAlapK , which should properly mean Send thou me to her with a message: but it is an inverted phrase; since the meaning is, be thou my messenger to her with this message [or rather with a message ]: and A^alikoniY A_ilayohaA biAls~alaAmi i. e. convey thou, or communicate thou, to her my salutation

; or be thou my messenger to her [ with salutation ]: and sometimes this [prep.] b is suppressed, so that one says, A^alikoniY A_ilayohaA Als~alaAma : sometimes, also, the person sent is he to whom the message is sent; as in the saying, A^alikoniY A_ilayoka Als~alaAma [virtually meaning receive thou my salutation; but literally] be thou my messenger to thyself with salutation. ; or] he uttered a cry in order that she should do the same. (TA.) The sportsman, coming to a place in which he thinks the young one of a gazelle or [wild] cow to be, utters a cry like that of her young one; and the mother, hearing it, if she have a young one, thinks the cry to be that of her young one, and follows the cry. [ More, and most, busy &c.]. A^a$ogalu mino *aAti Aln~iHoyayoni [ More busy than she who was the owner of the two skins of butter ] is a prov. [mentioned in the TA]: she was a woman of [the tribe of] Teym-Allah: she used to sell clarified butter, in the Time of Ignorance; and Khowwát Ibn-Jubeyr El-Ansáree came to her, demanding to buy clarified butter of her, and saw no one with her, and he bargained with her: so she untied a skin, and he looked at it: then he said to her, “ Hold thou it until I look at another: ” and she said, “ Untie thou another skin: ” and he did so, and looked at it, and said, “ I desire other than this; therefore hold thou it: ” and she did so: and when her hands were [thus] occupied, he assaulted her, and she was unable to repel the him. (Meyd.)
